title: Modules and Immutability
summary: import and export, and the habit of never changing data in place.

steps.title: Modules
body: Real projects split code into files called **modules**. Each file has its own scope; only what it **exports** is visible to others. This is like C# `public` plus `using`, but per file.
```ts
// math.ts
export const TAX = 0.08;
export function addTax(n: number) { return n * (1 + TAX); }
export default function round2(n: number) { return Math.round(n * 100) / 100; }
```ts
// cart.ts
import round2, { addTax, TAX as RATE } from "./math";
import type { Cart } from "./types";   // types only: erased at run time
console.log(round2(addTax(10)), RATE);
- **Named exports** are imported by name in braces. Prefer them: they rename safely and autocomplete well.
- A **default export** is imported with any name you like. Next.js uses it for pages: `export default function Page()`.
- `import type` brings in types only.
Exercises here stay in one file, so you will not write imports, but every Next.js file you read will start with them.

steps.prompt: `utils.ts` contains `export function slug(s: string) { ... }` and `export default function title(s: string) { ... }`. Which import is correct?
steps.explain: The default export comes first, without braces, under any name. Named exports go in braces and must match the exported name.

steps.prompt: Match each line to what it does.
pairs: imports a type only, erased at run time

steps.title: Why immutability
body: React and Next.js decide what to re-render by checking whether a value is a **different object** (`oldState !== newState`). If you mutate the existing array, it is still the same object, and the screen does not update. So the rule is: **never change data in place, make a new copy with the change**.
```ts
// mutating (avoid)          // immutable (do this)
list.push(item);             const next = [...list, item];
list.splice(i, 1);           const next = list.filter((_, j) => j !== i);
list[i].done = true;         const next = list.map((t, j) => j === i ? { ...t, done: true } : t);
list.sort(cmp);              const next = list.toSorted(cmp);
obj.count++;                 const next = { ...obj, count: obj.count + 1 };
`Object.freeze(obj)` makes mutation fail at run time (shallowly), and TypeScript's `readonly` (module 5) makes it a compile error.

steps.prompt: Does it mutate the original array?

code: const before = [{ id: 1, done: false }, { id: 2, done: false }];
const after = before.map(t => (t.id === 2 ? { ...t, done: true } : t));
steps.explain: Unchanged items are reused (the same object); the changed item is a new object. This structural sharing is what makes immutable updates cheap.

steps.title: Immutable list helpers
prompt: Write three functions that never mutate their input:
- `added(list, item)`: a new array with `item` at the end
- `removedAt(list, index)`: a new array without the element at `index`
- `replacedAt(list, index, item)`: a new array with that element replaced
All are generic: `added<T>(list: readonly T[], item: T): T[]`.
starter: function added<T>(list: readonly T[], item: T): T[] {
function removedAt<T>(list: readonly T[], index: number): T[] {
function replacedAt<T>(list: readonly T[], index: number, item: T): T[] {
solution: function added<T>(list: readonly T[], item: T): T[] {
function removedAt<T>(list: readonly T[], index: number): T[] {
function replacedAt<T>(list: readonly T[], index: number, item: T): T[] {
return list.map((x, i) => (i === index ? item : x));
template: Dojo.check("does not mutate a frozen array", false, String(e));
hints: `filter((_, i) => i !== index)` and `map((x, i) => i === index ? item : x)`.

steps.title: Update a nested object
prompt: State is shaped `{ user: { name: string; prefs: { theme: string; fontSize: number } }; version: number }`.

Write `setTheme(state, theme)` returning new state with `user.prefs.theme` changed and `version` increased by 1. Nothing in the old state may change, and `state.user.prefs` must be a **new** object in the result (spread each level you change).
